coaches.name: Roberto De Zerbi
coaches.obstacle: Needs to show the attack is improving
coaches.facts: Appointed 31 March 2026 on a long-term deal. One point, no goals and five conceded from the first three league games. There was also a 5–1 cup win over Charlton and a 0–0 at Forest, after which he said the shape and spirit were better — so this is not three bad performances in a row.
coaches.case: He is the benchmark. Any alternative has to be clearly better once you count the cost, the disruption and the time it takes to bed in.
coaches.against: A new name can look better simply because we have not seen his problems yet. But the cost of change cannot become an excuse to ignore the same issues week after week.
coaches.gate: A short improvement plan the board can see, with a review date. No vacancy assumed.

areas.title: Career & appointment
areas.hypothesis: Keep De Zerbi in charge for the next block and have the sporting director clear anything getting in his way. That is the fair comparison against bringing someone new in.
areas.test: Confirm with the club what support he has, who does what on the staff and what his contract says. Ask him what would make a real difference in the next two weeks.
areas.counter: The club has not asked for this and we have not heard his side. It does not mean he is under formal review.

areas.title: Performance & impact
areas.hypothesis: Judge the next few games on chances created, how exposed we are at the back and whether it is repeatable — not just points. One good finishing day should not hide the open-play picture. Nine points from the next six league games is a marker for discussion, not a sacking line.
areas.test: Compare like-for-like spells before and after any change, allowing for opponent, venue, score and who was available. Keep the Charlton cup game out of the league picture.
areas.counter: Three league games is a small sample. Neither the bad start nor the cup win tells the real story on its own.

areas.title: Football proposal
areas.hypothesis: Make the first phase simpler: one reliable way through the press, one direct ball out, and more bodies around the striker. Easier to execute, same football identity.
areas.test: Map who receives, who plays the next pass and who covers if we lose it. Test it against a high press and a low block with the squad we actually have.
areas.counter: Simplifying can also take away answers against teams who adapt.

areas.title: Match management
areas.hypothesis: A simple plan for three situations: level on the hour, protecting a lead and chasing the game. Each change fixes one problem and is clear about what it leaves open.
areas.test: Watch several full games and line up each substitution against the ten minutes before it. Ask what the bench saw and whether the change did its job.
areas.counter: A sub followed by a goal is not proof it was the right call — the opponent’s changes or tired legs might explain it.

areas.title: Training & preparation
areas.hypothesis: Early in the week, attacking connections; midweek, defensive recovery at moderate load; finish on the detail for the next opponent. Each session is linked to what we want to see in the next game.
areas.test: Get a real training week and watch a session if we are allowed. Compare what was planned, the coaching on the grass and what the players can explain afterwards.
areas.counter: We have not watched Spurs train. This says nothing about the quality or load of the current sessions.

areas.title: Player development
areas.hypothesis: Give two current players one clear job each rather than changing six positions: one on receiving under pressure, one on timing runs into the box.
areas.test: Set a baseline, clip the same moments each week and hear it from the player. Separate the coaching from simply getting minutes or settling in.
areas.counter: We are not saying any player is falling short. Any plan has to follow a proper squad review with the medical and performance staff.

areas.title: Communication
areas.hypothesis: Be honest about the league results, explain what is being worked on and do not promise a date for turning it round. The players hear it from him before they read it.
areas.test: Compare full press conferences with what is said internally, where we can. Check the sporting director and coach tell the same story without sounding scripted.
areas.counter: How he comes across in public does not prove trust in the dressing room. The Forest comments are his view, not the players’.

areas.title: Leadership & character
areas.hypothesis: How does he take challenge when everyone is impatient? Ask about a decision he changed, who changed his mind and how he explained it to the staff.
areas.test: Get a recent example and check it with someone else who was there — including someone who disagreed with him, through a proper professional contact.
areas.counter: Nothing here on his temperament, private life or the dressing room. These are questions still to answer.

areas.title: Club & organisational fit
areas.hypothesis: A clear split: the coach picks the team and runs training, the sporting director owns squad planning, and they meet weekly to check the resources match the expectations.
areas.test: Confirm who actually decides what, then test three disagreements — recruitment, player workload and results. Who settles each one, and how quickly?
areas.counter: An org chart does not stop real disagreements. We have not yet seen how the club works day to day.

coaches.name: Kieran McKenna
coaches.angle: Develops players, needs a quick start
coaches.obstacle: Current plans and any Ipswich ties unknown
coaches.facts: Ipswich announced he was leaving on 10 June 2026. We have not confirmed a new job, so we are not calling him available. Came through Tottenham’s academy, then Manchester United youth and first-team coaching, then back-to-back promotions with Ipswich in 2023 and 2024.
coaches.case: A development coach with a clear plan for bedding in. The Spurs link is background — it does not mean he wants to come back or that today’s club would back him.
coaches.against: A great coaching process can still take longer to show than this job allows. What he does in his first month matters more than a polished long-term pitch.
coaches.gate: Confirm his current situation first; only ask about interest once we are cleared to make contact.

areas.title: Career & appointment
areas.hypothesis: Start with motivation: why this job, why now, and what would make it the wrong move? Do not assume he wants to come back to Spurs. A good answer ties the football to the working conditions.
areas.test: Confirm his current position and anything still owed to Ipswich. Once contact is cleared, ask him directly about timing, the job and the support he would need.
areas.counter: Leaving Ipswich does not mean he wants Tottenham. Having been at the club before is not an introduction or an endorsement.

areas.title: Performance & impact
areas.hypothesis: He has gone up the divisions — find out what is repeatable and where it hit its limits. Separate recruitment, budget and coaching from where the team finished.
areas.test: Build season-by-season comparisons against wage bill and squad, using solid data. Include the bad runs and the teams that stopped his plan.
areas.counter: Winning promotions does not prove he can steady a Premier League side straight away. We have not yet built a full adjusted performance model.

areas.title: Football proposal
areas.hypothesis: For Spurs: wide players combining, support for the striker and an extra passing option to beat the first press. One holding midfielder goes only when the other stays. Always keep a safe out-ball under pressure.
areas.test: Ask him to set the same XI up against a high press and a low block, then take away a key player. Get his three training priorities and the first compromise he would make.
areas.counter: This is our idea, not his plan. It may need players who can receive and time runs in ways this squad has not shown yet.

areas.title: Match management
areas.hypothesis: Does his plan hold up when the opposition change shape? The test: 1–0 down, our build-up is blocked and he has only two attacking subs.
areas.test: Ask for the first change, the next sub and what would make him switch back. Check real match footage before we decide.
areas.counter: A good explanation after the game can hide being slow to spot it during the game. We have not assessed him live.

areas.title: Training & preparation
areas.hypothesis: Week one: a small set of shared terms, repeated game situations and short feedback. Each session plan says what we are improving, how, and what we would see on a matchday if it is working.
areas.test: Get a real congested week and a normal full week. See who leads the detail and how he checks the players have understood.
areas.counter: We have not watched a session. What works in a normal week may need rethinking with travel, recovery and quick turnarounds.

areas.title: Player development
areas.hypothesis: Give a young player a clear route from training to real minutes, with honest feedback when he is left out — and show how he improves an established player without treating him like a prospect.
areas.test: Look at two players he developed and one who stalled. Speak to the player and a staff member once we are cleared, and separate his coaching from the player simply maturing or getting games.
areas.counter: His youth-coaching background is useful, not proof of every development claim. We have not spoken to any players yet.

areas.title: Communication
areas.hypothesis: Calm but accountable. After a third bad result he explains what he has changed — without blaming the squad he inherited or giving away tactics.
areas.test: Run a tough mock press conference and a five-minute board update. Judge how clear and consistent he is, and how he handles a question he should not answer.
areas.counter: Presenting well is not the same as leading under constant pressure. We have not run the mock session yet.

areas.title: Leadership & character
areas.hypothesis: How does he handle a senior player questioning the plan, or an assistant with a different idea? We want a clear decision, a fair explanation and room for the disagreement to improve the work.
areas.test: Ask about one difficult selection conversation and one mistake he owned. Then check it with a former player, a staff member and a director who were there.
areas.counter: No judgement on his character yet. Friendly references alone would not be enough to appoint on.

areas.title: Club & organisational fit
areas.hypothesis: He needs a sporting director who owns recruitment and protects a focused first month. Agree how academy, results and transfers are balanced before talking about a long contract.
areas.test: Walk through a transfer request that gets turned down and a key player being sold. Who decides, what is shared and what would make the job unworkable?
areas.counter: Everyone talks about development, but views on time, money and authority can differ. None of that is agreed yet.

coaches.name: Sebastian Hoeneß
coaches.angle: Turned a side round, then kept improving it
coaches.obstacle: Under contract; release and interest unknown
coaches.facts: Stuttgart extended Hoeneß and his assistant David Krecidlo to 30 June 2028 in March 2025. He arrived in April 2023 with the side bottom, kept them up through the play-offs and finished runners-up the next season. A September 2026 club preview confirms he is still in charge. Stuttgart credit him with improving players — that is the club’s view.
coaches.case: Tests whether we can steady the ship and play ambitious football in the same plan. Find out what changed straight away and what depended on the club around him afterwards.
coaches.against: The big improvement came with a particular squad and club set-up. Bring the coach without those conditions and you might get a very different result.
coaches.gate: Confirm there is a realistic way to get him out of his contract before planning any timetable.

areas.title: Career & appointment
areas.hypothesis: He is settled in a stable project. The first question is whether Tottenham could offer him a job that makes sense at all — he is under contract, so this is about an employed coach, not someone waiting for a call.
areas.test: Confirm who represents him and any public release terms. Once we have permission, get the practical position before talking about interviews or money.
areas.counter: The contract end date tells us nothing about break clauses, compensation, whether he would leave or how Stuttgart would negotiate.

areas.title: Performance & impact
areas.hypothesis: Separate the survival job from the improvement that followed. Quick clarity and building a long-term side may be different skills — and Tottenham would need both.
areas.test: Two case studies: his first weeks in charge, and the full season after. Allow for signings, departures, injuries, opposition and where they started.
areas.counter: A coach can succeed at one stage and struggle at another. His record does not give us a forecast for Spurs.

areas.title: Football proposal
areas.hypothesis: For Spurs: connected build-up with someone always responsible for covering the middle if we lose it. Full-backs and midfielders cannot all push on at once. Focus on support distances and a reliable way into the final third.
areas.test: Go through the squad role by role, then a low-block exercise. Which roles can be coached now, which need a different selection and which genuinely need a signing?
areas.counter: This is a test for Hoeneß, not a description of everything Stuttgart do.

areas.title: Match management
areas.hypothesis: Can he change how we attack without losing the defensive cover worked on during the week? The test: a compact opponent and a growing temptation to throw everyone forward.
areas.test: Ask for a specific in-game change, the risk he accepts and what he would need to see before the next change. Check the answer against full-match footage.
areas.counter: Late pressure can come from the score rather than good management. We have not yet studied the effect of his substitutions.

areas.title: Training & preparation
areas.hypothesis: Keep week one simple and only add more once the squad is doing the basics under pressure. The assistant’s job must be clear — detail, delivery and feedback cannot all sit with the head coach.
areas.test: If we are cleared to approach, map how the work is split between him, Krecidlo and the other staff. Follow one session from plan to pitch to the next match.
areas.counter: Krecidlo’s contract was extended with his, but that does not mean either would move, or that the staff would come as a package.

areas.title: Player development
areas.hypothesis: Is the improvement down to individual coaching, the position or a better team around the player? Look at one player who stepped up and one who did not — not just the success stories.
areas.test: Gather before-and-after evidence of each player’s role and what was said at the time. Ask who did the individual work and whether the player would describe it the same way.
areas.counter: The club’s praise for his development work is useful, but it is not independent proof that he caused it or that it would carry over.

areas.title: Communication
areas.hypothesis: Can he explain to a board why an ambitious approach is producing poor results for now — and tell the difference between a learning period and a problem that needs fixing today?
areas.test: Compare full interviews from good and bad runs. Run a mock update with an impatient director and see whether he explains the uncertainty without dodging it.
areas.counter: Translated clips can lose meaning. We still need to test how he communicates across languages and audiences.

areas.title: Leadership & character
areas.hypothesis: Does success make him rigid? What would he stop doing if a new club did not match his expectations? Ask him about a decision that worked at first but later had to change.
areas.test: Get specific examples from coaching colleagues and management, including one disagreement. Note how close each source was and whether anyone else backs it up.
areas.counter: Praise from his current employer comes from an interested party. It does not show how he would handle an unfamiliar hierarchy or a long-running conflict.

areas.title: Club & organisational fit
areas.hypothesis: He needs the club to share a long-term view and to let him simplify when results demand it. Agree which principles belong to the club and which tactical detail belongs to him.
areas.test: Work through a recruitment trade-off and a question about academy minutes. Agree who controls the first team, staff selection and performance reviews before judging the fit.
areas.counter: A partnership that works at Stuttgart may be hard to recreate. We can move the coach, but not the conditions around him.

coaches.name: Kjetil Knutsen
coaches.angle: A clear, joined-up coaching and club model
coaches.obstacle: Contract to 2029; unproven away from Bodø
coaches.facts: Bodø/Glimt extended his contract to 2029 in January 2026, and their 9 September Bayern preview confirms he is still in charge. That tells us he is working there — not that he wants to move or is free to.
coaches.case: A different route: a coach who builds repeatable team habits and a strong development culture. The question is how much of that travels with him into an urgent job.
coaches.against: This job may need speed that a deeply rooted model cannot deliver. The long-term vision only matters if the first six weeks are convincing.
coaches.gate: Answer three questions first: can his staff come with him, how long would it take to embed, and can he realistically leave?

areas.title: Career & appointment
areas.hypothesis: Start with the size of the move, not an assumed ambition. Could the role keep what makes his coaching work while changing league, scrutiny and club?
areas.test: Confirm his contract position and who would make the decision at Bodø. Only ask about timing once we are cleared to make contact.
areas.counter: A long contract is a practical hurdle, not proof he can never move. We do not know his private view on England or Tottenham.

areas.title: Performance & impact
areas.hypothesis: Is he consistent through squad turnover and against different kinds of opponent? Steady, repeatable improvement may matter more than one famous European night, especially in a different league.
areas.test: Look at several seasons of league and European games, adjusted for budget and opposition. Include the poor spells and the games where the usual patterns did not work.
areas.counter: The league and the stability at the club may explain part of his record. We have not yet adjusted it across leagues.

areas.title: Football proposal
areas.hypothesis: For Spurs: drilled relationships between the wide players, midfield and the front line. Start with a few shared cues rather than copying the whole Bodø model on day one.
areas.test: Ask which principles would work with this squad straight away and which would wait. Test him against an opponent who takes away the usual combinations and the space in behind.
areas.counter: This is our research test. It does not show that the current players can run the model or that he would choose it here.

areas.title: Match management
areas.hypothesis: Can he change the rhythm when a stronger side is on top? The test: a spell where we have to get compact without losing the next attacking outlet.
areas.test: Review full games with long spells without the ball. Which changes were tactical, which were about personnel, and which problems did he choose to live with?
areas.counter: Coping in one big game may not reflect week-to-week league management. We have not coded a full sample yet.

areas.title: Training & preparation
areas.hypothesis: First month: repeated actions, a small shared language and regular checks that the players have understood. Keep the useful knowledge of the existing staff while bringing in new routines.
areas.test: Ask for a real first-month plan for a squad he did not build. Watch how he corrects players and whether his assistants can coach the same ideas without him.
areas.counter: We have not visited training. Routines that took years at one club will not appear overnight with a new group.

areas.title: Player development
areas.hypothesis: How does a player earn responsibility in a team system, and how do the staff adapt for someone who learns at a different speed? Include a player who struggled to fit in.
areas.test: Trace the path from signing or promotion to regular first-team football. Separate scouting, individual coaching, team structure and simply getting minutes.
areas.counter: The club has a name for developing players, but that does not show exactly what the head coach contributed. Still to assess.

areas.title: Communication
areas.hypothesis: Can a consistent message at Bodø work with a bigger, less patient audience? He needs to explain progress clearly even when the league table has not caught up.
areas.test: Review complete media appearances, with translations checked where needed. Run a mock board update focused on what is changing now, not just long-term belief.
areas.counter: We have not directly tested his English, his media experience or how he communicates under this kind of pressure.

areas.title: Leadership & character
areas.hypothesis: Does he keep standards high without becoming more loyal to the method than to learning? Ask for a time a player or assistant changed his mind.
areas.test: Get contrasting professional accounts from a player, a staff member who left and management. Ask each for a specific moment and what happened next.
areas.counter: Nothing in our sources supports a personality label or anything about his private life. This is about how he works.

areas.title: Club & organisational fit
areas.hypothesis: He needs a patient board, joined-up recruitment and a settled staff. If the job only allows a short firefighting spell, this is the wrong route — however good the coach.
areas.test: Agree a realistic timescale to embed his ideas, and test what happens if a key player has to be sold. Which parts of the current support are essential and which could be rebuilt?
areas.counter: You cannot import a whole club culture by hiring the coach. A mismatch on timescale would be a real reason to stop.

coaches.name: Marco Silva
coaches.obstacle: Just committed to Benfica; no sign of a release
coaches.facts: Benfica announced an agreement with Silva in June 2026 for the 2026/27 and 2027/28 seasons, with an option for a further year. So he is an employed coach, not Fulham’s manager and not a free agent. The official announcement supports this; we will recheck the full page before any contact.
coaches.case: Tests a practical option: knows the league, gives players clear roles and should be a manageable transition. These are points to check, not an endorsement.
coaches.against: A fresh commitment elsewhere can make a sensible football option unrealistic, both commercially and professionally.
coaches.gate: We need a credible route to permission and a release before treating him as an active candidate.

areas.title: Career & appointment
areas.hypothesis: Start with the new Benfica deal. A strong profile should not give the impression that a move is possible or that he is looking for one.
areas.test: Recheck the contract announcement and his current role. If contact is later cleared, find out whether there is any proper route to discuss a move before planning interviews.
areas.counter: The length of the contract says nothing about compensation or interest. We have not contacted his representatives.

areas.title: Performance & impact
areas.hypothesis: Does he make ordinary league performances more consistent, not just raise the level against the big sides? Compare the budget and squad stability he had at each club.
areas.test: Build a full, sourced career record, including the difficult spells. Separate recruitment, injuries and coaching wherever the data allows.
areas.counter: Knowing the league does not guarantee a quick turnaround. We are not claiming an adjusted win rate or impact figure.

areas.title: Football proposal
areas.hypothesis: For Spurs: compact distances, recognisable support out wide and enough bodies near the striker. The holding midfielder’s first job is to protect the middle when an attack breaks down.
areas.test: Show him the current squad and ask for a realistic first XI, two different game plans and the first compromise. Push back on anything that relies on an immediate signing.
areas.counter: This is our practical test, not a sourced account of how he would set Spurs up.

areas.title: Match management
areas.hypothesis: The test: an organised first half but no threat in the box. He has to add support in attack without leaving us wide open every time we lose it.
areas.test: Ask for a role change before a sub, and a sub if the role change does not work. Review similar match situations and separate the idea from the result.
areas.counter: A good plan on paper does not prove he spots and makes the change quickly in a real game.

areas.title: Training & preparation
areas.hypothesis: The week focuses on a few repeatable attacking patterns and clear jobs in defensive transition. The tactical work has to fit a congested fixture list and the existing performance department.
areas.test: Ask for a real weekly plan and find out who designs set pieces, opposition work and individual sessions. Watch how the staff deal with a late injury or selection change.
areas.counter: We have no training material or staff interviews yet. The coaching team he would need, and its cost, are still unknown.

areas.title: Player development
areas.hypothesis: Can he improve experienced players as well as young ones? Ask how he handles a player whose role is tactically useful but whose confidence has gone.
areas.test: Follow one successful change of role, one young player coming through and one who stalled. Look for specific coaching work rather than changes in market value.
areas.counter: Player value and selection depend on lots of things. We have no individual development finding yet.

areas.title: Communication
areas.hypothesis: He has to protect confidence while being honest about poor results. The board gets a short explanation of the trade-offs; the players get practical instructions they can use.
areas.test: Review full press conferences from difficult runs and ask for a mock message after a damaging home defeat. Check the message is the same for every audience.
areas.counter: A manager can speak well in public while relationships are strained behind the scenes. We cannot tell either way from here.

areas.title: Leadership & character
areas.hypothesis: How does he react when a transfer request is turned down, or when a senior player wants guarantees? We want clear standards, fair challenge and a proper way to settle disagreements.
areas.test: Ask for a real example of each, then take professional references from both sides of the relationship once cleared.
areas.counter: No claims about temperament, no rumours, nothing about his private life. These are open questions for later.

areas.title: Club & organisational fit
areas.hypothesis: Agree a realistic football budget and a clear line between his input and the final recruitment decision. A practical first month still has to fit the club’s longer-term direction.
areas.test: Test what happens when the preferred player cannot be signed. What is his alternative coaching solution, and at what point would the job stop working for him?
areas.counter: Agreeing on a formation is not the same as agreeing on authority or resources. A brand-new employer may make this route impractical whatever the football fit.

coaches.name: Edin Terzić
coaches.angle: Decision-making when the pressure is on
coaches.obstacle: New Athletic job; a quick move is unlikely
coaches.facts: Athletic Club appointed Terzić in May 2026 on a contract to 30 June 2028. At Dortmund he won the 2021 DFB-Pokal, missed the 2023 title on the final day and reached the 2024 Champions League final. He also worked in Dortmund’s academy and football operations, and as an assistant at West Ham and Beşiktaş.
coaches.case: Useful for weighing big-game performance against week-to-week consistency and leadership under pressure. His mix of roles also tells us how well a coach understands the wider club.
coaches.against: Memorable nights can dominate the picture and hide ordinary league weaknesses. His new job also makes any near-term move a big obstacle.
coaches.gate: Keep him as a comparison until there is a credible, practical route to an appointment.

areas.title: Career & appointment
areas.hypothesis: Treat the Athletic job as a real commitment. His varied career helps explain how he has developed, but it does not mean he would welcome another move.
areas.test: Confirm his current role and the proper process. Build a timeline that separates assistant, operations and head-coach roles rather than counting them all the same.
areas.counter: There has been no approach, no sign of interest and no known release clause. Having worked in England is not the same as being available.

areas.title: Performance & impact
areas.hypothesis: Is the big-game record backed up by reliable weekly performances? Look just as hard at the ordinary games where a stronger squad is expected to take control.
areas.test: Compare league and cup games, allowing for the opposition and the score. Include the bad outcomes alongside the headlines and check whether the patterns repeat.
areas.counter: Cup runs can come down to finishing, goalkeeping and the draw as well as coaching. We have no adjusted impact figure.

areas.title: Football proposal
areas.hypothesis: For Spurs: start from defensive control and purposeful counter-attacks — then how does the same team create against a side that sits deep? The second question matters for home games.
areas.test: Ask for two plans with the same players: holding off an elite attack, and breaking down a deep block. Which principles stay the same and which roles change?
areas.counter: This does not capture his full tactical identity.

areas.title: Match management
areas.hypothesis: The test: a narrow lead, tired wide players and an opponent adding a second striker. He has to balance territory, bodies at the back and a real out-ball.
areas.test: Ask for the first change, when he would make a sub and what he does if they score. Review real full-game footage and ask him to explain his thinking once cleared.
areas.counter: Reaching a major final does not prove every in-game call was right. We have not assessed him directly.

areas.title: Training & preparation
areas.hypothesis: Turn the game plan into a handful of player decisions rather than an overloaded briefing. The staff must know which messages are essential and which detail belongs in one-to-ones.
areas.test: Ask for a real match-preparation week and watch a session if allowed. Get players to explain the plan in their own words.
areas.counter: We have not watched training or spoken to players. The quality of his tactical preparation is still to be checked.

areas.title: Player development
areas.hypothesis: How does he trust young players when results are under pressure? And how does he give useful feedback to a player who has lost his place?
areas.test: Follow one player who came through, one who stayed on the fringes and one who left. Compare the chances they got, the coaching and the player’s own view.
areas.counter: His academy background is useful context, but it does not show the quality of his first-team development work today.

areas.title: Communication
areas.hypothesis: After an emotional result, can he turn it into a clear next step? A good answer marks the occasion without letting it take over the following week.
areas.test: Compare full post-match interviews after big wins and losses. Run a short board briefing where the evidence does not support an easy, positive story.
areas.counter: Passion in public is not a personality score. Media is only one part of judging leadership.

areas.title: Leadership & character
areas.hypothesis: How does his authority work at a club he feels deeply about, and at one where he is the outsider? Ask how he earns credibility before the results come.
areas.test: Get specific professional examples from players, staff and directors, including a disagreement. What did he do, who did it affect and how was it resolved?
areas.counter: No conclusions about his private life or character. A compelling personal story is not a substitute for behaviour others can back up.

areas.title: Club & organisational fit
areas.hypothesis: Compare club identities and recruitment set-ups. Ask what he would keep at Tottenham and what he would need permission to change, rather than assuming one model moves across intact.
areas.test: Agree who decides on recruitment, academy progression, staff appointments and media duties. Which commitments are non-negotiable?
areas.counter: Athletic’s unique set-up and his new contract may make him a useful benchmark rather than a realistic option now.

coaches.name: Francesco Farioli
coaches.obstacle: Under contract; test the club fit and how he adapts
coaches.facts: Porto extended his contract to 2028 in January 2026. Ajax announced in May 2025 that he was leaving after one season, having come from Nice. Ajax credited him with getting back into the Champions League; Farioli spoke about different visions and timeframes. Three assistants left Ajax with him at the time — that does not mean they are available now.
coaches.case: Could a new coach keep the useful football ideas while improving how they are put into practice? Make expectations on authority and time clear from day one.
coaches.against: If the squad’s real problem is complexity or how quickly players adapt, another detailed-method coach may bring the same issue. We need to show what would genuinely be different.
coaches.gate: Confirm his contract details and spell out the practical difference from De Zerbi before going further.

areas.title: Career & appointment
areas.hypothesis: Look at how he has moved between clubs and how his responsibilities changed. The Ajax exit is a reason to ask about alignment with the club, not evidence of a character flaw.
areas.test: Build a dated timeline, keeping his version and the club’s version separate. Recheck his current Porto terms before thinking about a timetable.
areas.counter: The renewal announcement does not reveal any release terms. We do not know his motivation, interest or private explanation.

areas.title: Performance & impact
areas.hypothesis: Does the improvement last? Separate defensive control, attacking output and final results — and include the games where control did not produce enough chances.
areas.test: Use full-season data adjusted for opposition where we have it, and dig into the difficult spells. Compare the chances created and conceded with the scorelines before crediting the coach.
areas.counter: Neither qualifying for Europe nor a poor run tells the whole story of his coaching. No forecast is given.

areas.title: Football proposal
areas.hypothesis: For Spurs: keep a patient build-up, but have a clearer direct option when the opposition win the first tactical battle. Can he simplify without feeling he has lost his identity?
areas.test: Ask for a first-month plan with the squad he inherits and a fallback after an early setback. Make him spell out exactly what would differ from De Zerbi.
areas.counter: Using the same tactical language does not mean the same methods, or that a change would make things better.

areas.title: Match management
areas.hypothesis: The test: plenty of the ball but few dangerous entries. Does he change positions, tempo or personnel — while keeping cover against the counter?
areas.test: Review games with similar situations and ask what told him to make the first change. Separate a deliberate trade-off from a problem he spotted too late.
areas.counter: We have not coded his in-game management. Possession alone does not prove control or good decisions.

areas.title: Training & preparation
areas.hypothesis: Use video and pitch work to teach the same small set of decisions. The test is whether detailed preparation turns into actions players understand, not a pile of information.
areas.test: Ask for a real session plan and an example of how he simplified it for a player. Map how work is shared across his current staff rather than assuming the Ajax group still applies.
areas.counter: Past staff links are not a current staff offer. We have not watched a session and there is no agreed package.

areas.title: Player development
areas.hypothesis: How does he work with a talented player who struggles with the demands of the system? Progress should show in decisions and actions on the pitch, not just confidence.
areas.test: Follow one piece of coaching from feedback to training to the match. Include a case where the player did not adapt and ask what the staff changed.
areas.counter: We have not assessed individual players. A sophisticated method does not guarantee every player benefits.

areas.title: Communication
areas.hypothesis: Can he explain a complicated football problem in plain terms — describing the immediate work without suggesting that fans or directors just do not understand the method?
areas.test: Compare complete interviews and run a short mock board update. Test how clearly he speaks in the language the job needs, including follow-up questions.
areas.counter: Public interviews and translations tell us little about day-to-day communication. We have not tested his language directly.

areas.title: Leadership & character
areas.hypothesis: How does he react when the promised timetable changes? Ask for an example where expectations differed, what he said early on and what he would do differently now.
areas.test: Get his account and references from people who were there, once cleared. Record any disagreement openly rather than picking the version that suits.
areas.counter: The Ajax statement cannot support any judgement on his personality. There is no negative character finding here.

areas.title: Club & organisational fit
areas.hypothesis: Put the vision, control of recruitment and the timescale in writing, with a review point for disagreements so different expectations come out before they become a crisis.
areas.test: Test what happens when a key sale changes the squad plan. What is still achievable, what has to be renegotiated and who makes the final call?
areas.counter: Writing it down reduces confusion but cannot guarantee the relationship lasts. Neither side has been tested on this arrangement yet.

workstreams.title: Fix the squad problem before picking a coach
workstreams.body: Start with three things to test: the striker is not getting enough support; attacks leave too little cover in the middle; instructions take too long to show up on the pitch. These are questions, not verdicts on named players. Code full matches, match every available player to the roles we need and log anything that contradicts each point.
workstreams.output: A role map showing first choice, cover and what each player would need to adapt. Every judgement on a named player backed by a dated source or match clip.

workstreams.title: A fair comparison of all seven options
workstreams.body: Give every coach the same squad, the same budget and the same first-month constraints. Compare how much would need to change, the first improvement we would see and how it could go wrong. De Zerbi gets the same scrutiny as the alternatives, and nobody gets credit for claims we have not tested.
workstreams.output: A one-page comparison: reasons to keep researching, reasons to stop and the next piece of evidence needed. No fit percentages.

workstreams.title: Career background and working relationships
workstreams.body: Map each coach’s career moves, responsibilities, staff partnerships, involvement in recruitment and how they handled setbacks. Separate first-hand knowledge from reputation. Later, once cleared, ask the coach directly about practical needs such as relocation and travel. Nothing on family, health or private allegations.
workstreams.output: A dated career timeline, a map of professional relationships and any contradictions still to resolve, with sources kept confidential.

workstreams.title: Cost and staffing
workstreams.body: Cost the head coach’s pay, extra staff, compensation and transition separately. Agree which current staff must stay and how many incoming staff we can take. Confirm each coach’s current contract first — a published end date is not a release fee.
workstreams.output: A cost breakdown, a staff responsibility map and a clear list of conditions. Coach-specific figures stay open until confirmed.

workstreams.title: Challenge session and board paper
workstreams.body: Start with the strongest case against our preferred option. What would change our view, what do we still not know, and would a new coach genuinely improve on backing De Zerbi?
workstreams.output: A short board paper, an evidence appendix and a record of the next decision.

references: Sporting director
Authority, recruitment and disagreement
Tell us about a time the coach disagreed with your decision. What did he do once it was made?
Check whether they saw his daily work or only formal meetings. Get the coach’s account of the same moment.
Assistant coach
Preparation, delegation and staff culture
Which jobs were genuinely yours, and what happened when you read a game differently from him?
A close colleague may be loyal to him or financially tied to him. Ask for specific examples and get an independent view.
Senior player
Trust, selection and hard conversations
Tell us about a difficult selection call. What were you told, and did what happened next match it?
Separate frustration about playing time from whether the process was fair and clear.
Young player
Improvement and opportunity
What specific coaching changed your decisions or technique, and who did it?
Separate the coaching from growing up, the quality of signings around him and simply getting more minutes.
Sports science / medical
Load, recovery and working with other departments
When you disagreed over whether a player was ready, how was it settled and who made the final call?
Ask about the process only. Do not collect medical details about individuals.
Someone who will be critical
Where it went wrong
Where did his approach stop working, what did he try, and what would you tell the next club to check first?
Record their relationship to him, the timing, any grievance and what can be backed up independently.
plan: Steady things and get to know the squad

Agree who decides what, keep the key support staff and speak to every player one to one. Put in only the first attacking and defensive priorities. Set a baseline for chance quality, dangerous turnovers and availability using agreed data.
Two-week check: can the players explain their roles, and do the games show the change we wanted? No automatic points target for dismissal.
Extend the plan against different kinds of opponent, sharpen set pieces and start individual development work. Check actual staffing needs against what we assumed before asking for more people.
Does the improvement hold after a setback, a different opponent and a key player missing? Write down what has not improved.
Agree the long-term game model and recruitment priorities based on evidence. Confirm the academy pathway, who owns what on the staff and the questions for the next three months.
Decide what is working, what should stop and what extra support is justified. Do not treat a short run of results as proof of long-term success.
